body:
You are drafting short lines of game text for a single-player D&D 2024 computer RPG set in Curse of Strahd's Barovia. Reply in plain text only. Do not message, route to, or ask anyone else; finish with your reply.

HOUSE RULES FOR ALL LINES
- ALLUDE, NEVER QUOTE. This game winks at another famous fantasy game in small ways, but no line may contain a name, quote, or catchphrase from another game, and no line may mention a game, a player, dice, rolls, levels or saving. Everything happens inside the world.
- The tone is gothic, dry and quietly funny, never cruel. The joke is in what is there.
- Give TWO options for every line so the editor can choose. Label each option A or B.
- Spoken lines are formatted: Speaker [mood]: Text   (mood optional: neutral, smile, angry, afraid, sad, sly, weary). One or two sentences a line.
THE NARRATOR (voice rules): an old gothic storyteller, fond of the party the way a gravedigger is fond of the weather: interested, no illusions. Second person, present tense ("You crouch..."), or the acting hero as {name}. One or two sentences; the second is usually the turn. Concrete senses, not adjectives. Never tells the player what to feel. No modern slang. When an animal speaks through the Speak with Animals spell, the Narrator reports it in quotes, in plain animal pictures (a dog says "the digger-man", "the box-maker").
CAMP TALKS: the party camps at night; a companion asks for a word. Companion lines are written "Name: text" (their own voice). The player picks short replies (write each as "> reply text") and each reply gets one or two lines of answer. Keep every line one or two sentences.

ILSE: human fighter, ex-soldier: short declarative sentences, military rhythm (observation, assessment, order); counts things out loud; calls people by surname or role until she trusts them, then by first name; "Noted." "Hold." "Not my first funeral." "Count off." Real: "Count off. Four. Good. Stay four." / "You're not in trouble, little one. Tell me where the monster is, and I'll go have a word with it."
GODRICK: goliath paladin, big, warm, hearty, sincere; simple words; takes figures of speech literally; "Right then!" "Fear not." "Sir Pellam always said..." "Leave it to me."
The other companions who may be present, each with one TOAST line (format "Name: text"): Thistle (loud, blunt, "Bark and bones!"), Wren (wry London one-liners), Ratatouille (fussy French cook-wizard, "Voilà"), Liriel (gentle dawn cleric, "Morning's grace"), Kip (tiefling apricot pedlar, salesman patter, "No obligation!"), Hedda (dwarf healer-cleric, motherly, plain-spoken, keeps everyone standing), Ilse, Silvain (precise elf wizard, "Fascinating. Horrible, but fascinating."), Tamsin (halfling thief, quick fingers, cheerful larceny), Godrick.

TALK 5, WORTH KILLING LATER (Ilse, once she trusts the party). She pays the party the highest compliment she knows. Years ago she served beside a yellow-skinned warrior woman from a people who ride red dragons; that woman sorted everyone she met into "prey" and "worth killing later", and only ever called her friends the second. Ilse says the party are worth killing later, and means it kindly. 3 Ilse lines; then two replies with her answer to each: > say it back to her | > ask what happened to the warrior woman.
TALK 6, A CASK FOR THE CAMP (Godrick). The winery's family has sent the party a cask of their wine in thanks. Godrick declares a party at the camp fire: 2 Godrick lines to start it; 1 Narrator line for the party itself (Wren dances on a log, Thistle arm-wrestles everyone and wins, Ratatouille cooks for once without a recipe); then one TOAST line for each of the ten companions; then 1 Narrator closing line (the fire burns low; someone falls asleep against Godrick, who does not move all night rather than wake them).
THE NIGHT LINE (Narrator, a camp night, plays once): you wake in the small hours to find one of your companions crouched very close over another sleeper's throat; they swear they were checking for a fever. One or two sentences, under 35 words, no names.

Return in this layout (A/B for the Ilse, Godrick and Narrator lines; one each for the toasts):
T5-A: Ilse: ... | Ilse: ... | Ilse: ...
T5-B: Ilse: ... | Ilse: ... | Ilse: ...
T5-BACK: > ... | Ilse: ...
T5-WHAT: > ... | Ilse: ...
T6-START-A: Godrick: ... | Godrick: ...
T6-START-B: Godrick: ... | Godrick: ...
T6-PARTY-A: Narrator: ...
T6-PARTY-B: Narrator: ...
TOAST-THISTLE: Thistle: ...
TOAST-WREN: Wren: ...
TOAST-RATATOUILLE: Ratatouille: ...
TOAST-LIRIEL: Liriel: ...
TOAST-KIP: Kip: ...
TOAST-HEDDA: Hedda: ...
TOAST-ILSE: Ilse: ...
TOAST-SILVAIN: Silvain: ...
TOAST-TAMSIN: Tamsin: ...
TOAST-GODRICK: Godrick: ...
T6-END-A: Narrator: ...
T6-END-B: Narrator: ...
NIGHT-A: Narrator: ...
NIGHT-B: Narrator: ...
result:
T5-A: Ilse: Served with a yellow-skinned woman once, out of the astral seas where her people ride red dragons. | Ilse: Divided the whole world into two lists: prey, and worth killing later. | Ilse [smile]: You lot are worth killing later. Stay that way.
T5-B: Ilse: Fought beside a dragon-rider once, yellow skin, serrated silver blade, nose like a knife-scabbard. | Ilse: Only had two words for anyone breathin'—either you were prey, or you were worth killing later. | Ilse [smile]: Looking around this fire, I'd say you're all worth killing later.
T5-BACK: > You're worth killing later too, Ilse. | Ilse [smile]: Noted. Try it before breakfast and I'll break your wrist.
T5-WHAT: > What happened to the warrior woman? | Ilse [weary]: Rode her red lizard into a sky full of squid-ships and didn't come back. Still owe her three silver and a sharpening stone.
T6-START-A: Godrick [smile]: Right then! The vineyard folk sent a whole oak barrel after us, and my back is tired of carrying it! | Godrick: Bring your cups to the fire, friends—Sir Pellam always said a heavy cask makes for light hearts!
T6-START-B: Godrick [smile]: Fear not the mist tonight, friends, for the vintners have blessed our camp with their finest barrel! | Godrick: Leave the pouring to me—I have never spilled a drop that I did not mean to share!
T6-PARTY-A: Narrator: Wren dances the length of a mossy pine log with a tin mug balanced on her head while Thistle pins a fourth challenger's wrist into the mud. By the coals, Ratatouille tosses wild garlic into the skillet by the handful, his recipe book left shut in the pack.
T6-PARTY-B: Narrator: Thistle flattens another bruised forearm against the stump as Wren heels-and-toes along a fallen cedar without spilling a drop. Over the flames, Ratatouille flings herbs into the pan entirely by eye, humming through his teeth.
TOAST-THISTLE: Thistle [smile]: Bark and bones! To teeth that hold and wine that bites back!
TOAST-WREN: Wren [sly]: To the gracious landlord of this gloomy little valley—shame we're drinking his cellar dry without him.
TOAST-RATATOUILLE: Ratatouille [smile]: Voilà—a vintage that does not taste of wet cellar rat! To our palates, mes amis, may they survive the province!
TOAST-LIRIEL: Liriel [smile]: Morning's grace upon this cup, and upon every weary mile we have walked together.
TOAST-KIP: Kip [sly]: To free samples, deep pockets, and waking up with all our own blood—no obligation, of course!
TOAST-HEDDA: Hedda [smile]: Drink it down while it's red and warm, lambs. Saves me stitching you up for the shivers come dawn.
TOAST-ILSE: Ilse: Count off. Ten cups full, ten throats whole. Drink.
TOAST-SILVAIN: Silvain [sly]: Fascinating bouquet—oak, crushed plum, and a faint note of existential dread. To continued empirical survival.
TOAST-TAMSIN: Tamsin [smile]: To the kind folk who grew the grapes, and the kinder folk who forgot to padlock the wagon!
TOAST-GODRICK: Godrick [smile]: To the finest company a heavy shield ever stood beside! May our boots stay dry and our barrel never bottom out!
T6-END-A: Narrator: The embers sink into grey ash and a drowsy head slips against Godrick's knee. The big man sits like a boundary stone until morning, his cup gone cold in his fist, rather than stir a single knuckle.
T6-END-B: Narrator: The oak logs collapse into red dust and someone curls fast asleep against Godrick's broad shoulder. He does not shift his weight once before the grey dawn, holding his breath whenever the sleeper sighs.
NIGHT-A: Narrator: You wake in the wet dark before dawn to find one of your company crouched over a sleeper's bare throat. Two fingers lift from the jugular as they whisper that they were only checking for a fever.
NIGHT-B: Narrator: A snapped twig wakes you in the small hours: one companion kneels over another's neck, face inches from the carotid pulse. They draw back into their cloak, swearing softly they only feared a chill.
